newsitem.title: zaire: Rebels vow to restore Zaire's fabled mineral wealth.
newsitem.headline: Rebels vow to restore Zaire's fabled mineral wealth.

text.p: Zaire's rebel alliance paused in its war to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko on Wednesday to sign a $1 billion deal it hopes will resurrect the fabled mineral wealth of Shaba province.

Its goal is to relaunch the broken-down mines of Shaba, formerly known as Katanga, which once worked the world's richest deposits of copper, cobalt and zinc but slumped into decrepitude under Mobutu's government.

The agreement with America Mineral Fields Inc., the biggest to date by Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Forces for the Democratic Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL), was signed in recently captured Lubumubashi, capital of Shaba.

"Everybody is going to profit from these agreements. Above all, investment must profit the people of this country and especially those in the region where resources are developed," Kabila's finance minister Mwana Nanga Mawanpanga said.
Initial injections of cash would also help pay for the war to topple Mobutu, "which is our number one priority", he added.

Kabila forces now control about half of Zaire, a country the size of western Europe. Kabila left Lubumbashi for Cape Town on Wednesday amid expectations of a dramatic breakthrough in his bid to end Mobutu's 32 years in power.
"We want to liberate this country -- all of it," said Mawanpanga. "If we fail after giving so much hope, no one will forgive us."

America Mineral Fields chief Jean-Raymond Boulle said he supported the rebel cause and had full confidence that what his company regards as the de facto government of rebel-held territories would become the new government of Zaire.

The deal involves deposits and mines under the control of Zaire's state-owned Gecamines which will be exploited and modernised by America Mineral Fields as a joint venture, with the U.S. company controlling 51 percent and Kabila's alliance holding a minority blocking share of 49 percent.

Three separate accords cover the exploitation of copper- cobalt tailings at Kowlezi, the rehabilitation of mines at Kipushi, near the Zambian border, and creation of what Boulle called the world's largest zinc smelter at Kipushi with a capacity of 200,000 tonnes a year.
The company also planned to build an acid plant with an annual output of 400,000 tonnes to replace the costly Gecamines practice of importing acid to the middle of Africa for the refining process.
These plants made up the largest single element of Wednesday's contracts with a value estimated at between $550 and $650 million.
In addition, America Mineral Fields Inc. gained exploration rights to deposits in the Kipushi region and was study a further tailings deal.

Mawanpanga said Boulle's company had submitted the winning tender for these projects last December but corrupt politicians had intervened in February this year, attemping to have it awarded to minerals giant Anglo American Corp.
"We want to send a message to the world that from now on there will be open and transparent dealings," he said. The era of corruption, bribes and backdoor manoeuvring was over, he added.
